Many women first owned a small phone with buttons, often called a **feature phone** or, in everyday Nigerian speech, a "small phone" or "torchlight phone". It makes calls, sends text messages (SMS), and lasts days on one charge. A **smartphone** does all of that, but it is really a small computer with a touch screen. It connects to the internet, runs programs called **apps**, takes good photos and videos, and can be updated with new features.

Android and iPhone

Every smartphone runs an **operating system**, the main software that controls the phone. There are two you will meet. **Android** is made by Google and is used by many brands, such as Samsung, Tecno, Infinix, itel, Xiaomi, Nokia and others. **iOS** runs only on Apple's **iPhone**. Most phones sold in Nigerian markets run Android, so the steps in this course use Android. Menu names differ a little from brand to brand, so if you cannot find a setting with the exact name used here, look for a similar word or use the search box at the top of the Settings app.
The four numbers that matter most
When you buy a phone, the seller may show you a box or a page full of numbers. You do not need to understand all of them. Four numbers tell you most of what you need to know.
Specification
What it means
A simple guide
Storage (ROM), for example 64 GB
The space for apps, photos, videos, voice notes and documents. GB means gigabyte.
More is better. Small storage fills up fast with WhatsApp photos and videos.
RAM, for example 4 GB
The phone's working memory. It decides how many apps can run smoothly at the same time.
Low RAM makes a phone slow and makes apps close by themselves.
Battery, for example 5,000 mAh
mAh (milliamp-hours) tells you how much charge the battery can hold.
A bigger number usually means longer use between charges.
Android version, for example Android 14
The version of the operating system. Newer versions get security updates for longer.
Avoid very old versions; some apps stop working on them.

Two more things are worth asking about. First, **dual SIM**: most phones sold here take two SIM cards, so you can keep, for example, one line for family and one for business. Second, the **camera**: the megapixel number (MP) is printed on many phones, but a bigger number does not always mean better photos. If you can, take a test photo in the shop and look at it closely.
Worked example: comparing two phones at the shop
For example, Hauwa in Kano has saved money for a phone. In the shop, two Android phones cost about the same. She will use it for WhatsApp, photos of her customers' orders and online classes.
Phone A: 64 GB storage, 4 GB RAM, 5,000 mAh battery, Android 14.
Phone B: 32 GB storage, 2 GB RAM, 4,000 mAh battery, an older Android version.
She compares storage: Phone A has 64 GB, which is twice Phone B's 32 GB.
She compares battery: 5,000 mAh minus 4,000 mAh is 1,000 mAh more charge in Phone A, which is 25% more (1,000 divided by 4,000).
She checks RAM: 4 GB is twice 2 GB, so Phone A will switch between WhatsApp, the camera and a class app more smoothly.
She asks the seller to switch Phone A on in front of her, checks that the screen, both cameras and the charging port work, and asks for a receipt and the warranty terms in writing.
Hauwa chooses Phone A. It costs about the same but has double the storage, double the RAM, 25% more battery capacity and a newer Android version, so it will stay useful for longer.
New, used and refurbished
**New** phones come sealed in the box with a warranty. Check the box seal before you pay.
**Used** phones, often called "UK used" or "fairly used", cost less but may have weak batteries or hidden faults. Test everything before paying.
A **refurbished** phone has been repaired and checked by a seller. Ask what was replaced and how long the seller's guarantee lasts.
Buying a used phone safely

Buy from a shop you can return to, not from a stranger on the street. Ask the seller to remove their Google account and reset the phone in front of you, otherwise the phone may lock and ask for the old owner's account after a reset. Insist on a written receipt with the seller's name and address. A price far below the market is a warning sign: the phone may be stolen.

Finally, think about how you will use the phone. If you mostly chat on WhatsApp and make calls, a modest phone with good battery is enough. If you will take many product photos, attend video classes or run a small online business, put your money into more storage and RAM first, because those two numbers decide how long the phone stays fast.

There is also a **proximity sensor** near the earpiece. It turns the screen off when you hold the phone to your ear, so your cheek does not press buttons during a call. If your screen stays dark after a call, a thick screen protector or dirt over this sensor may be the cause.
SIM cards and the SIM tray

Your **SIM card** connects you to your network, for example MTN, Airtel, Glo or 9mobile. It holds your phone number, not your photos or apps. SIM cards come in three sizes, standard, micro and nano, and most new phones take the smallest, nano. Many SIM packs today are cut so you can press out the size you need. Some newer phones also support an **eSIM**, a SIM built into the phone that your network sets up for you.
Switch the phone off first.
Find the SIM ejector pin that came in the box (a straightened small safety pin can work, but be gentle).
Push the pin straight into the tiny hole beside the tray until the tray pops out a little, then pull it out with your fingers.
Place the SIM in its slot with the gold contacts facing down and the cut corner matching the shape of the slot.
Slide the tray back in the same way it came out, until it sits flat with the edge of the phone.
Switch the phone on and wait for the network name and signal bars to appear.
Do not force it

Never push the pin into the microphone hole by mistake; the microphone is usually a tiny hole on the bottom edge, while the SIM pin hole sits right next to the tray outline. If the tray does not slide in smoothly, take it out and check that the SIM is lying flat.
Your IMEI: the phone's own identity number

Every phone has an **IMEI** (International Mobile Equipment Identity), a 15-digit number that identifies that exact handset. Your phone number belongs to the SIM; the IMEI belongs to the phone. A dual-SIM phone has two IMEI numbers, one for each SIM slot. To see it, open the phone dialler and type *#06#. The numbers appear at once, without pressing call. The IMEI is also printed on the box and in Settings under About phone.
Worked example: making a phone record card

For example, Chinwe in Onitsha has just bought a dual-SIM Android phone. A friend lost her phone last year and had no details to give when she reported it, so Chinwe decides to record hers on day one.
She dials *#06# and two 15-digit numbers appear: IMEI 1 and IMEI 2. She writes both down carefully and checks each one has 15 digits.
She checks the box label and confirms the numbers match the ones on the screen.
She writes the brand, model and colour, her two phone numbers, the shop name and the date of purchase.
She photographs the receipt and the box label, and keeps the paper card in the folder where she keeps important documents at home.
She also emails the photo to herself so it is safe even if the phone is lost.
Chinwe has one card with everything needed to prove the phone is hers and to describe it exactly if it is ever lost or stolen: model, both IMEIs, both numbers and the receipt.

A touch screen responds to the light touch of a finger. You do not need to press hard. Most new users press too long or too hard at first; with a little practice your fingers learn quickly. In this lesson you will go from a phone that is off to a phone you can move around confidently.
A woman touching the screen of a large phone
Light, short touches are all a touch screen needs.
On, off and restart
**To switch on:** press and hold the power button for about two to three seconds until the brand logo appears, then let go.

**To switch off or restart:** press and hold the power button until a menu appears, then tap Power off or Restart. On some newer phones, holding the power button calls a voice assistant instead; on those, press power and volume down together, or pull down quick settings and tap the power icon.
**A quick press** of the power button only turns the screen on or off. The phone is still on.
Restarting fixes many small problems, such as a frozen app or no network signal. Make it a habit to restart your phone about once a week.
Two different locks: SIM PIN and screen lock

When the phone starts, you may meet two different locks. The **SIM PIN** protects the SIM card: it is asked for only when the phone starts or the SIM is moved to another phone. If you enter it wrongly three times, the SIM locks and asks for a PUK code, which you get from your network with proof that the line is yours. The **screen lock** protects the phone itself every time the screen comes on. Set it in Settings, under Security, Lock screen, or Screen lock.

A smartphone gets to the internet in two ways. **Mobile data** comes through your SIM card from your network, and you pay for it with data bundles. **Wi-Fi** comes from a wireless router, for example at an office, a church, a hotel, or a pocket device called a MiFi, or from another phone that shares its connection (a **hotspot**). Your phone can use either, and it prefers Wi-Fi when both are available.

Reading the status bar

The thin strip at the very top of the screen is the **status bar**. It is like the dashboard of a car: it tells you, before you open any app, whether you can get online. The exact look changes between phones, but the meaning is the same.

What it tells you
Signal bars (like steps)
How strong the network signal is. More filled bars, better signal. On dual-SIM phones there are two sets.
4G, LTE, 5G, 3G, H+ or E
The type of network connection. 4G, LTE and 5G are fast; H+ and 3G are slower; E is very slow and struggles even with WhatsApp photos.
Small up and down arrows
Data is actually moving. If there are no arrows next to 4G, mobile data may be switched off.

You are connected to Wi-Fi. A small exclamation mark or a cross means connected but no internet.
Airplane
Airplane mode is on: calls, SMS and mobile data are all off.

Roaming: you are using another network, often abroad, and charges can be high.
Switching on mobile data
Swipe down twice from the top to open quick settings.
Tap the Mobile data tile until it is highlighted. Small arrows should appear beside the network type.
On a dual-SIM phone, go to Settings, then Network or Connections, then SIM manager or SIM cards, and choose which SIM is used for mobile data. Choose the SIM where you buy your data bundle.
To save data when you are not using the internet, you can switch Mobile data off from the same tile; calls and SMS still work.
Joining a Wi-Fi network
Long press the Wi-Fi tile in quick settings to open the Wi-Fi list.
Switch Wi-Fi on. The phone shows the names of networks nearby, with a padlock on those that need a password.
Tap the network name you were given, for example the name printed on a MiFi or told to you by the office.
Type the password exactly, with capital and small letters as given. Tap the eye icon to see what you typed.
Tap Connect. Under the name you should see Connected. The phone will join this network by itself next time.
Worked example: WhatsApp messages stuck on the clock

For example, Grace in Port Harcourt sends three messages to her supplier, but each one shows a small clock instead of ticks, meaning it has not left her phone. She reads the status bar step by step before calling anyone.
She looks at the top of the screen: four signal bars and 4G are showing, so the network signal is fine.
She notices there are no small arrows beside 4G. She opens quick settings and sees the Mobile data tile is grey (off). She must have tapped it by accident.
She taps Mobile data on. Arrows appear, but the messages still show the clock.
She checks her data balance in her network's app (she could also use the balance code printed on her SIM pack) and sees her monthly bundle expired yesterday.
She buys a new bundle. Within a minute, the clocks change to ticks and the messages are delivered.
Two separate problems, data switched off and an expired bundle, were found and fixed in a few minutes by reading the status bar in order: signal first, then data switch, then balance.

A smartphone is often the most valuable thing in a woman's handbag, and it holds her contacts, photos, business chats and bank apps. A few simple habits can make it last years longer. Most phone damage comes from four things: heat, poor charging, drops and water.
A phone battery symbol
Smartphone batteries are lithium-ion: they last longer when kept away from heat and poor-quality chargers.
Charging safely
Use the charger that came with the phone, or a good-quality replacement from a shop you trust. Very cheap chargers can overheat and damage the battery.
Charge on a hard, open surface such as a table. Do not charge the phone under a pillow, on a bed or inside a bag, where heat cannot escape.
Never charge or handle a plugged-in phone with wet hands, and keep it away from water while charging.

When power supply is unstable, for example when power returns after an outage or when switching between grid and generator, unplug the charger and wait for the power to settle. A surge protector extension gives extra protection.
Unplug the charger from the wall socket when you finish; do not leave a live cable hanging where children can reach it.
A swollen battery is dangerous

If the back of your phone is lifting, the screen is being pushed out, or the phone gets very hot and smells strange, stop using it and stop charging it at once. Switch it off, keep it away from anything that can burn, and take it to a qualified repairer for a new battery. Never press, pierce or try to flatten a swollen battery.
Habits that help the battery last

Heat is the main enemy of phone batteries. Avoid leaving the phone in the sun, on a car dashboard, or near a cooking fire. Try not to let the battery run down to zero often; charging when it falls to about 20% is a good habit. Some phones have a setting, usually under Battery, that stops charging before 100% to protect the battery when it is charging for long periods. Turning down screen brightness and closing apps you are not using also saves charge.
Worked example: how many charges from a power bank?
For example, Aisha in Abuja travels often and wants a power bank. The shop label says 10,000 mAh. Her phone's battery is 5,000 mAh, which she found in Settings under About phone.
She divides the power bank size by her battery size: 10,000 divided by 5,000 equals 2.
She learns that this 2 is the best case on paper. Some energy is always lost as heat while charging, so in real use she will get fewer than two full charges.
For her old phone with a 3,000 mAh battery, the paper figure would be 10,000 divided by 3,000, about 3.3 charges, again less in practice.
She chooses a power bank from a known brand with clear labelling, and charges it on a table, not in her bag.
Aisha expects a bit less than two full charges from a 10,000 mAh power bank for her 5,000 mAh phone, and is not disappointed or misled by the label.
Screen, case and cleaning
A **tempered glass screen protector** takes the crack instead of your real screen, and costs far less to replace.
A **case** with raised edges protects the corners, where most drops land.

To clean, switch the phone off, then wipe with a soft, lint-free cloth. For sticky marks, slightly dampen the cloth with water. Never spray liquid straight onto the phone, and avoid bleach or harsh cleaners.
Clean the charging port gently with a dry soft brush or by blowing; never push in a pin or needle.
If the phone gets wet

Some phones carry an **IP rating**, for example IP67 or IP68. The first number is protection against dust (6 means dust-tight). The second is protection against water: 7 means tested for immersion up to 1 metre for a limited time, and 8 means tested deeper than 1 metre under the maker's conditions. Even a rated phone is not made for swimming, and protection weakens with age and drops.
Take it out of the water at once and switch it off. Do not charge it.
Remove the case and the SIM tray, and wipe the outside dry.
Leave it switched off in open air to dry for a long time. Do not use a hairdryer, an oven or direct sun, because heat damages the phone.
If it will not work properly afterwards, take it to a qualified repairer and tell them it got wet.

Fewer than two full charges, because some energy is lost as heat
Five full charges
Half a charge

Bola's phone fell into a bucket of water. What should she do first?
Charge it to see if it still works

Switching off and not charging reduces the risk of short circuits. Heat from a hairdryer or sun can cause further damage.

Use your phone to reach people clearly and safely: calls with all the in-call controls, text messages and USSD codes, your first steps on WhatsApp, and a contact list that is backed up and easy to search. The module ends with the habits that make you a trusted, responsible communicator.

Writing numbers in international format

In Nigeria we usually write mobile numbers with 11 digits starting with 0, such as 0803 555 0142 (a made-up example). Apps like WhatsApp, and people calling from abroad, need the **international format**: the plus sign, the country code, then the number without the first 0. Nigeria's country code is 234.
Worked example: saving a customer's number correctly
For example, Joy sells fabric in Aba. A customer writes her number as 0803 555 0142 on a paper. Joy wants it to work for calls, SMS and WhatsApp, including when Joy travels.
She counts the digits: 0803 555 0142 has 11 digits.
She removes the first 0, leaving 803 555 0142, which is 10 digits.
She puts +234 in front: +234 803 555 0142.
She checks the total: 3 digits of country code plus 10 digits gives 13 digits after the plus sign.
She saves it under the customer's name and taps call to test that it rings.
The number +234 803 555 0142 works for calls and SMS in Nigeria, works from abroad, and is found correctly by WhatsApp.

Emergency calls

If you do answer, let the caller introduce themselves first and do not confirm your full name, address or bank details to someone you cannot identify. If an unknown number keeps calling at odd hours, use Recents to block it. **SMS** (Short Message Service) is the oldest kind of text message. It works on every phone, needs no internet and no data bundle, only airtime and network signal. That is why banks, schools, hospitals and networks still use SMS for alerts and reminders. On a smartphone, SMS lives in the **Messages** app, which is a different app from WhatsApp.
Text message bubbles on a phone screen
SMS works with only network signal and airtime, which makes it the backup when data runs out.
SMS vs WhatsApp message

Sending an SMS
Open Messages and tap Start chat, the plus sign or the pencil icon.

How long can an SMS be?

One SMS holds up to **160 characters** of ordinary letters, numbers and common punctuation. A character is any single letter, digit, space or mark. If your message is longer, the phone splits it into parts and joins them on the other phone, but each part then holds only **153 characters**, because a little space is used to join them. If you add an emoji or certain special characters, the whole message switches to a different coding and one SMS holds only **70 characters**, or **67 per part** when split. Networks usually count each part separately, so long messages and emoji can cost more.
Worked example: counting SMS parts for a customer reminder
For example, Ruth runs a small tailoring shop in Jos and sends SMS reminders to customers who do not use WhatsApp. She wants to know how many parts her messages use.
Message 1 is plain text with 140 characters. 140 is not more than 160, so it is 1 SMS.
Message 2 is plain text with 300 characters. It is more than 160, so it splits into parts of 153. 300 divided by 153 is about 1.96, so it needs 2 parts.
Message 3 has 100 characters including one smiley emoji. The emoji makes the limit 70. 100 is more than 70, so it splits into parts of 67. 100 divided by 67 is about 1.49, so it needs 2 parts.
She removes the emoji from Message 3. Now 99 plain characters fit in 1 SMS.
By keeping reminders plain and under 160 characters, Ruth sends each one as a single SMS. Removing one emoji halved the parts for Message 3.
Reading an alert SMS

Bank alerts usually show the account (partly hidden), whether money came in (credit, often CR) or went out (debit, often DR), the amount, a short description and the new balance. Treat an SMS alert as a notice, not as proof. Before you release goods to a customer who says they have paid, open your bank or payment app and check that the money is really in your balance. Fake alert messages can be typed by anyone.
USSD codes: menus without the internet

**USSD** codes start with a star and end with a hash, such as the *#06# you used to find your IMEI. Networks and banks use USSD codes for checking airtime and data balance, buying bundles and making transfers. You type the code in the Phone dialler and press call; a menu appears on screen and you reply with numbers. Unlike SMS, a USSD session is not saved in your Messages, and it times out if you wait too long.
Get balance and bundle codes from your network's official website, app or SIM pack, not from strangers.
Bank USSD codes can move money. Never dial a code someone sends you "to receive a payment" or "to verify your account".
Protect your bank USSD PIN like your ATM PIN, and never say it aloud in a crowded place.
Delete codes you received

One-time codes (OTPs) arrive by SMS when you log in or pay. They are for you alone. If you receive one you did not ask for, someone may be trying to get into your account: do not share it, and change your password or call your bank using its official number.
Promotional messages and sender names

Alongside alerts from your bank and school, you will receive promotional SMS from networks and businesses, often from names instead of numbers. A sender name on an SMS can be copied by fraudsters, so a message that looks like it comes from your bank but asks you to click a link or call a strange number deserves suspicion. Your real bank will not ask you to update your BVN, unlock your account or claim a prize through an SMS link. If in doubt, ignore the link, and contact the bank through the number printed on your card or inside its official app.
Keep Messages tidy
Long press a conversation and tap the bin icon to delete it. Many phones also let you archive promotional messages so bank and school alerts stay easy to find.

WhatsApp is the app most Nigerians use every day to chat, share photos and voice notes, call family abroad and run small businesses. It uses the internet, so it needs mobile data or Wi-Fi. This lesson covers your first week. The WODDI course WhatsApp for Communication and Business goes much further, into groups, Status and the WhatsApp Business app.
A phone showing a chat conversation
Your first goal is simple: send a message, a voice note and a photo, and understand the ticks.
Installing and verifying
Open the **Play Store**, search for WhatsApp Messenger and check that the developer shown is WhatsApp LLC. Tap Install.
Open WhatsApp, agree to the terms, choose Nigeria and type your phone number without the first 0.

Type your name (this is what people see) and, if you wish, add a profile photo.

Your 6-digit code is your key

Anyone who gets your WhatsApp verification code can take over your account and message your contacts as you. Never send it to anyone, even a friend or someone claiming to be from WhatsApp. If someone asks for it, they are trying to steal your account.
Sending text, voice notes and photos
**New chat:** tap the green message icon at the bottom right, choose a contact, type in the message box and tap the green send arrow.

**Voice note:** press and hold the microphone icon, speak, then lift your finger to send. To record hands-free, slide your finger up to the padlock while holding; tap send when finished. Slide left while holding to cancel.
**Photo:** tap the camera icon in the message box to take a new picture, or the paperclip (or plus) icon, then Gallery, to send one you already have. You can add a caption before sending.
**Reply to a specific message:** swipe it to the right, then type your answer. Your reply shows the original message above it.
What the ticks mean
The life of a WhatsApp message
Clock: not sent yet
One grey tick: sent
Two grey ticks: delivered
Two blue ticks: read
Each step shows how far your message has travelled, from your phone to the other person's eyes.

A **clock** means the message has not left your phone, usually because there is no internet. **One grey tick** means it reached WhatsApp's system but not yet the other phone, often because their phone is off or has no data. **Two grey ticks** mean it arrived on their phone. **Two blue ticks** mean they opened the chat. If someone has switched off read receipts in their privacy settings, you will not see blue ticks even after they read. In groups, ticks turn blue only after every member has read.
Worked example: first voice note to a son in Lagos
For example, Mama Nkechi in Owerri has just set up WhatsApp. Her son Emeka lives in Lagos and has asked her to send voice notes instead of calling, so he can listen between meetings.
She opens WhatsApp, taps the green message icon and finds Emeka in her contacts.
She types "Good morning my son" and taps send. She sees a clock, then one grey tick, then two grey ticks within seconds.
She presses and holds the microphone, speaks for about 30 seconds about the family meeting, and lifts her finger. The voice note sends.
She taps the camera icon, takes a photo of the new chairs for the meeting and adds the caption "Chairs have arrived".
Twenty minutes later the ticks turn blue, and Emeka replies with his own voice note.
In one sitting Mama Nkechi sent text, a voice note and a photo, and could see from the ticks exactly when Emeka received and read them.
Voice and video calls

Open a chat and tap the **phone** icon at the top for a voice call or the **video camera** icon for a video call. These calls use data or Wi-Fi, not airtime, and work with family abroad. Video uses much more data than voice, so on a small bundle choose voice or connect to Wi-Fi first.
Small habits that save data and space

Every photo, video and voice note you receive is saved on your phone, and by default WhatsApp may download them automatically, using your bundle and storage. In WhatsApp Settings, open Storage and data and look at Media auto-download. Many people set photos to download on Wi-Fi and mobile data, but videos and documents to download only on Wi-Fi, then tap any video they actually want to see. This keeps both your data bundle and your storage under control, without missing anything important.
Turn on two-step verification on day one

In WhatsApp, open Settings, then Account, then Two-step verification, and create a 6-digit PIN you will remember. Add your email address. This stops someone who tricks you out of the SMS code from taking your account.

If it is messy, you waste time searching; if it is not backed up, one lost phone can wipe it out. In this lesson you will build a contact list that is tidy, searchable and safe.

Name contacts so you can find them

Many people save names like "Mummy Tolu" or "Aunty" or just "Mr". Six months later, nobody remembers who that is. Use a simple pattern: **first name, surname or role, and where or what**. For example: "Amina Bello Tailor Wuse", "Mr Okon Plumber", "Tolu Mum, School PTA". When you search, any of those words will find the person.

In the Contacts app settings, look for Default account for new contacts and set it to your Google account.

For example, Folake in Abeokuta is buying a new phone. Her old phone has 180 contacts stored on her SIM, collected over many years. She wants all of them on the new phone without retyping.

She opens Contacts and checks the count: 168. She searches for three people at random and finds each one.
All 168 cleaned contacts arrived on the new phone automatically, and they will survive any future phone change because they now live in her Google account.

Your phone lets one message reach hundreds of people in seconds. That power can help a community, for example a quick warning about a road closure, or cause real harm, for example a false rumour about a school, a person or a medicine. Being a responsible communicator means you pause, check and think about the people in the message as well as the people receiving it.
People exchanging messages online
Every forward passes your trust along with the message, so check it first.
Check before you forward

WhatsApp marks forwarded messages with a small **Forwarded** label, and messages that have been forwarded many times with a double arrow and **Forwarded many times**. These labels mean the person who sent it to you probably did not write it. Ask yourself four questions before you pass it on.
**Who first said this?** Is a real organisation or person named, and can you find the same news on their official page?
**When?** Old news is often recirculated as if it is new. Look for a date.
**Does it push me to act fast?** "Forward to 10 people", "before it is deleted" or "share urgently" are pressure signs.
**Who could be hurt if it is false?** A person, a business, a school or someone who follows wrong health advice.
Before you press forward
Pause
Find the original source
Confirm directly
Share, or delete
If you cannot find the source or confirm it, the safe choice is not to forward.
Worked example: the school closure message

For example, Patience in Benin City receives a forwarded message on Sunday night: "All primary schools in the state closed tomorrow by order of government. Forward to all parents." She is the secretary of her parents' WhatsApp group of 60 members.
She notices the Forwarded many times label and that no date, office or official name is given.
She checks the state government's official social media page and the school's own page: there is no announcement.
She calls the school's head teacher, whose number is on the school's letterhead. The head teacher says school opens as normal.

Instead of forwarding, she posts in the parents' group: "A message about schools closing tomorrow is going round. I called the head teacher: school is open as normal. Please do not forward the rumour."
Sixty families heard the truth from one checked source, and children were not kept at home by a false message. Patience's word now carries more weight in the group because she checks.
Consent: other people's pictures and words
Ask before posting a photo or video of someone else, especially in their home, at a hospital, or when they are upset.
Be extra careful with children's photos. Avoid showing school uniforms, school names or your home location next to a child's face.
Do not screenshot a private chat and share it in a group without the person's permission, unless you are reporting abuse or a crime to someone who can help.
Ask before adding someone to a group, and never share another person's number with a stranger.
Protect your own details

Keep your home address, your daily routine ("I close shop at 8pm and walk home alone"), travel dates, and photos of documents such as your NIN slip, ATM card or passport out of public posts and Status. Share live location only with people you trust and for a limited time. Never share PINs, passwords or one-time codes with anyone.
Polite habits that build trust
Call during reasonable hours unless it is urgent; send a message first if you are not sure.
Keep voice notes short and to the point; say the main thing first.
In groups, stay on the group's topic and reply privately to personal matters.
Read your message once before sending, especially when you are angry. You can always wait an hour.
When you made a mistake

Everyone forwards something wrong at least once. If you discover that a message you shared was false, say so in the same chat or group, briefly and without embarrassment: "I shared a message earlier about the market closing. It was not true, please ignore it." On WhatsApp you can also long press a recent message you sent and choose Delete for everyone, but people may already have read or forwarded it, so a clear correction is still needed. Correcting quickly shows others that checking matters, and it makes your future messages more trusted.
If someone harasses or threatens you

Do not reply to the abuse. Take screenshots that show the messages, the date and the sender's number or profile. Then block and report the sender: in WhatsApp, open the chat, tap the name at the top, then Block and Report. Tell someone you trust. If you feel unsafe or are threatened, take your screenshots to the police.

Online safety is not only about spotting scam messages. Much of it is quietly set up inside the phone itself. Six habits, set up once and checked from time to time, protect your photos, contacts, chats and money even when you make a mistake or lose the phone. This lesson walks through each one on an Android phone. The WODDI courses Internet Basics and Online Safety and Scam Awareness and Digital Trust go deeper into passwords and scams.
A woman beside a large padlock and shield
Most protection is switched on in Settings once, then works for you every day.
Habit 1: a real screen lock

You set this up in Module 1. Check it is a PIN of at least six digits, a password, or fingerprint backed by a PIN. Also set the screen to lock quickly, for example after 30 seconds, under Display, Screen timeout.
Habit 2: install updates

Updates fix security holes that criminals use. Open Settings and search for "software update" or "system update", then tap Check for updates. Connect to Wi-Fi or make sure you have enough data first, because updates can be large. You can also see how recent your protection is: in About phone, look for **Android security update** or **Security patch level**, which shows a date. If the date is more than a year old and no update is offered, the phone no longer receives security fixes; be extra careful with banking on it.
Habit 3: Google Play Protect

**Google Play Protect** checks apps on your phone for harmful behaviour. Open the Play Store, tap your profile picture at the top right, then **Play Protect**. It should say no harmful apps found. Tap the settings gear and make sure scanning is on. Most dangerous apps reach phones as APK files sent through WhatsApp links or download sites. Install apps only from the Play Store, and if your phone asks you to allow "install unknown apps", say no.
Habit 4: check app permissions

A **permission** is a door an app asks you to open: to your camera, microphone, location, contacts, photos or SMS. Open Settings, search "permission manager" (or go to Privacy, Permission manager) and look at each sensitive permission to see which apps have it. Ask: does this app need this to do its job? A camera app needs the camera. A torchlight or game app does not need your contacts or SMS.

Sensitive access the app does not need is a warning sign; sensitive access it does need should be limited to while you are using it.
Worked example: a torchlight app that wanted too much

For example, Funmi in Ilorin reviews her permissions after a friend's account was misused. She finds a free torchlight app she downloaded months ago, before she knew her phone had a flashlight in quick settings.
In Permission manager, she taps Contacts and sees the torchlight app listed. A torch does not need contacts: sensitive and not needed.
She taps Location and SMS and finds the same app again. Both are sensitive and not needed.
Her WhatsApp has Microphone set to Allow all the time. Voice notes need the microphone, but only when she is using WhatsApp, so she changes it to Allow only while using the app.
She uninstalls the torchlight app completely, since the flashlight tile in quick settings does the same job.
She runs Play Protect again: no harmful apps found.
One unnecessary app with access to her contacts, location and SMS is gone, and WhatsApp keeps only the access it really needs. The whole check took about ten minutes.
Habit 5: back up

Search Settings for "backup" and switch on **Backup by Google One** (or Google backup), which saves contacts, app data, call history and settings to your Google account. Use **Google Photos** with Backup switched on to keep your photos safe. For WhatsApp, open WhatsApp Settings, Chats, Chat backup, and choose a daily or weekly backup to Google Drive, on Wi-Fi only if data is costly. Free Google storage is limited, so check that backups are completing.
Habit 6: Find My Device

Search Settings for "Find My Device" and switch it on. If the phone is lost, you can sign in to Google's Find My Device from another phone or computer to see its last location, make it ring, or lock and erase it. Write down your Google email and password in a safe place at home, because you will need them when your phone is gone.
Put a reminder in your Clock or Calendar app to repeat this check once a month. It takes about ten minutes once everything is set up, because you are only confirming that nothing has changed.
After a lost or stolen phone

Act quickly: use Find My Device to lock it, call your network to block the SIM and get a replacement, and call your bank using its official number to block mobile banking. Then change your Google and email passwords from another device.

Worked example: the market list and a discount
For example, Esther in Makurdi buys provisions for her small shop. Prices are approximate and change often; she uses the Calculator to check the trader's total, a promised discount and her change.

A smartphone does not make money by itself. It helps you **show** what you sell, **reach** more customers, **take** orders and **receive** payment. Most women who earn with a phone already have a product or a skill: food, fashion, hair, tailoring, tutoring, cleaning, crafts or reselling. The phone makes that work visible beyond your street.

Getting paid safely
Photos and messages that sell

Customers decide quickly, so make each post do its job. Take product photos in daylight near a window or outside in shade, against a plain background, with the item filling most of the picture. Wipe the camera lens first with a soft cloth. Write the price, size or quantity, and how to order in the caption, for example: "Plantain chips, 150 g pack, 1,000 naira. Order by WhatsApp, delivery in Bodija on Tuesdays and Fridays." Reply to enquiries quickly and politely, and confirm every order in writing with the item, quantity, total price and delivery day, so there is no argument later.

Customers can pay you by **bank transfer** to your bank account, or to an account with a licensed mobile payment provider such as Opay, Moniepoint or PalmPay. Some businesses also send customers a **payment link** from services such as Paystack. Whichever you use, follow one rule: **an SMS, a screenshot or a customer's word is not payment**. Open your own bank or payment app and see the money in your balance before you release goods or start work. Use a separate account for business if you can, so your records stay clear.

Show product with price

Confirming payment inside your own app, before delivery, is the step that protects your money.
Worked example: plantain chips sold through WhatsApp

For example, Adunni in Ibadan makes plantain chips. Figures are approximate and for illustration. She sells each pack for about 1,000 naira, and her ingredients and packaging cost about 600 naira per pack. She posts on WhatsApp Status every morning and sells about 40 packs a week.
Profit per pack: 1,000 minus 600 equals 400 naira.
Weekly profit: 400 naira times 40 packs equals 16,000 naira.
Monthly profit over 4 weeks: 16,000 times 4 equals 64,000 naira.
She subtracts her phone costs for the business, data and airtime, plus delivery transport, about 5,000 naira a month: 64,000 minus 5,000 equals 59,000 naira.
She checks every transfer in her bank app before handing over chips, and writes each sale in a notebook: date, customer, packs, amount, paid yes or no.
Adunni earns about 59,000 naira a month after costs, and because she records each sale and confirms each payment, she knows the real figure rather than guessing.
Spotting fake "easy money" offers
Social media and WhatsApp are full of offers that promise income for very little work. Genuine work pays you; schemes take your money. Be suspicious of any offer with one or more of these signs.
You must **pay to join**, buy a "package" or pay a "registration fee" before you can earn.
You earn mainly by **recruiting** other people who also pay.
It promises a fixed high return, such as doubling your money, or daily profits with no risk.
You are paid small amounts at first for easy tasks (liking videos, rating products), then asked to deposit larger sums to "unlock" your earnings.
There is pressure to act now, and no real business address or registered company you can check.
If you have already paid

Stop paying more, even if you are told you will lose what you paid. Keep screenshots of chats, account numbers and receipts, and contact your bank at once through its official number. The WODDI course Scam Awareness and Digital Trust covers reporting steps in detail.
Start with what you already do

The fastest phone income usually comes from a skill or product you already have. Take five good photos of your work this week, write a clear price for each, and share them with people who already know and trust you.

The challenge is not finding content; it is choosing good content, managing data, and actually finishing.

When a search gives you many choices, start with the source that has a clear author, a recent date and a real organisation behind it. A long list of free courses is only useful if you finish one.

Anyone can publish online, so check before you believe or act, especially on health, money and law. Ask four questions: **Who** wrote it, and are they a real expert or official body? **When** was it written or updated? **What evidence** does it give, such as data or links to official sources? **Why** was it written: to inform, or to sell you something? For health information, trust official bodies such as the World Health Organization (who.int) and the Nigerian Federal Ministry of Health, and your own health worker, over social media posts.
Making data go further
**Download on Wi-Fi, watch later.** Many learning apps, including video apps, let you download lessons when you have Wi-Fi and watch offline.
**Lower the video quality.** In most video players, tap the settings gear and choose a lower quality such as 360p or 480p; for talking-head lessons you lose little.
**Use audio when the picture is not needed.** Lectures and talks work as audio while you cook or travel.
**Read text lessons.** Text uses far less data than video.
**Close other apps** that may be updating or playing videos in the background.
Plan your study time

Courses are finished by women who make study a fixed appointment, not something they do "when there is time". Pick a time that already exists in your day, for example after the children leave for school, during a lunch break, or after evening prayers, and protect 20 minutes. Put it in your Clock as a repeating alarm with a label.
Worked example: how long will this course take?

For example, Rahila in Jos wants to finish a 20-lesson WODDI course. Each lesson takes about 12 minutes to read, and each practice task takes about 15 minutes. She can study 20 minutes a day, five days a week.
Reading time: 20 lessons times 12 minutes is 240 minutes.
Practice time: 20 tasks times 15 minutes is 300 minutes.
Total: 240 plus 300 is 540 minutes.
Weekly study time: 20 minutes times 5 days is 100 minutes.
Weeks needed: 540 divided by 100 is 5.4, so about 5 and a half weeks.
Rahila plans for 6 weeks, giving herself a small buffer for busy days. If she only counted reading time (240 minutes, 2.4 weeks), she would have felt behind when the practice tasks took longer.
Study habits that make learning stick
The learning loop
Learn a small piece
Try it on your phone
Write a short note
Review next day
Each pass around the loop turns something you read into something you can do.
**Learn small:** one lesson at a time, not five in one night.
**Try it at once:** if the lesson is about bookmarks, bookmark something now.
**Write a note** in your own words, in a notebook or the Notes app. Writing helps memory.
**Review** yesterday's note for two minutes before starting a new lesson.
**Teach someone:** explaining a skill to a friend or your child shows what you have really understood.
Learn with others
A study partner or a small group that agrees to finish the same course by the same date is one of the strongest supports for finishing. Share one thing you learned each week in your group chat.

Finally, keep your phone ready for study: clear enough storage for downloaded lessons, charge it before your study time, and switch on Do not disturb for those 20 minutes so messages do not pull you away.
Certificates for sale

Be careful of websites that sell certificates without real assessment, or that ask for payment to "release" a free course certificate. Check who issues the certificate and whether employers in your field recognise it.

Your digital footprint and online reputation: what people find, and how to shape it
Explain active and passive digital footprints
Search for yourself and review what the public can see
Protect identity details such as your NIN, BVN and card numbers
Present a consistent, trustworthy profile across platforms

Every time you post, comment, join a group, shop online or even search, you leave a trace. Together these traces are your **digital footprint**. Customers, employers, scholarship panels, and sometimes fraudsters look at it. A good footprint builds trust before you even meet someone; a careless one can cost you an opportunity, or give criminals what they need to pretend to be you.
A profile card with a photo and details
Your profile photo, name and public posts form the first impression many people will have of you.
Two kinds of digital footprint
Active footprint
Passive footprint
Posts and photos you share
Comments and reviews you write
Your profile name and bio
Groups you join publicly
Location history apps record
Websites and searches you visit
Data apps collect quietly
What others post about you
You control your active footprint directly; you limit your passive footprint with privacy settings and care.
Your digital identity documents

In Nigeria, many official services are now tied to your **National Identification Number (NIN)**, and SIM cards must be linked to the owner's NIN. Your **BVN** (Bank Verification Number) links your bank accounts. These numbers, along with your card numbers, PINs and passwords, are keys to your identity and money. Never post photos of your NIN slip, ID card, passport, ATM card or any document showing these numbers, and do not send them on WhatsApp to people you do not know. If an official process needs them, use the organisation's own app, website or office.
Small settings that shrink your passive footprint
**Location history:** in your Google account settings, look at Timeline or location history and switch it off or set it to delete automatically if you do not need it.
**Ad personalisation:** in your Google account, under Data and privacy, you can turn off personalised ads.
**Photo location:** in your Camera settings, switch off location tags, so photos you share do not carry the place they were taken.
**Old accounts:** delete apps and accounts you no longer use, so your details are not sitting in services you have forgotten.

None of these settings stops you using your phone normally. They simply reduce how much is recorded about you without your knowledge. Combined with careful posting, they keep your footprint to what you choose to share.
See yourself as others see you
Open Chrome and search your full name in quotation marks, for example "Chiamaka Obi". Add your town or business name if the name is common.
Look at the first two pages of results and the Images tab.
Open each of your social media profiles while logged out, or ask a friend to look, to see what a stranger sees.
List anything you would not want a customer or employer to see.
Worked example: tidying a footprint before a job application
For example, Chiamaka in Enugu is applying for an administrative job and wants her online presence to support her application. She sets aside one evening.

She searches her name and finds her public Facebook profile, an old public post where she argued angrily with a stranger, and a photo of her holding her new ID card that a friend posted three years ago.
She deletes the angry post and changes the audience of her older posts to Friends, using Facebook's option to limit past posts.
She asks her friend politely to remove the ID card photo; the friend removes it the same day.
She updates her WhatsApp profile photo to a clear, smiling headshot and writes an About line: "Administrative assistant, Enugu. Organised, reliable."
She uses the same name and photo on WhatsApp and LinkedIn so a recruiter can tell they are the same person.
A search for Chiamaka now shows a consistent, professional profile, and no public image exposes her ID number. The whole tidy-up took about two hours.
Build a footprint you are proud of
Use the same name and a clear, recent photo on the platforms you use for work or business.
Write a short, honest bio: what you do, where, and how to reach you for business.
Share your work: finished products, happy customers (with their permission), skills you have learned.
Comment respectfully, even when you disagree. Screenshots last longer than anger.
Keep family life and children's details on private accounts.
If someone pretends to be you

If you find a fake account using your name or photos, do not argue with it. Screenshot the profile, report it to the platform as impersonation, and warn your contacts on your real account not to send money or details to the fake one.

Think too about what others post about you. Ask friends and family not to tag you in photos at home or in places you visit regularly, and in Facebook's settings you can choose to review posts you are tagged in before they appear on your profile. If a group or page shares your photo without consent, ask the admin politely to remove it, and report it to the platform if they refuse.
Do a footprint check twice a year
Put a reminder in your calendar every six months to search your name and review your profile photos and privacy settings.

Your rights and responsibilities online: data protection, complaints and respectful behaviour
List your rights under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023
Write a short request to a company about your personal data
Follow a complaint path from the company to the regulator
Practise the responsibilities that make you a good digital citizen

Being a **digital citizen** means you have rights online, as you do offline, and responsibilities to others. Nigeria has a law that protects personal information, the **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023**, and it set up the **Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)** to enforce it. Personal data means any information that identifies you, such as your name, phone number, photo, address, NIN, bank details or location.
A personal information card with a shield
Organisations that collect your data must handle it lawfully, and you can ask what they hold.
Your rights over your personal data
Right
What it means in practice
To be informed
Organisations should tell you what data they collect, why, and who they share it with, usually in a privacy notice
Of access
You can ask an organisation for a copy of the personal data it holds about you
To rectification
You can ask them to correct wrong or incomplete data
To erasure (to be forgotten)
You can ask them to delete your data in certain situations
To restrict processing
You can ask them to limit how they use your data in certain situations
To data portability
You can ask for your data in a form you can take to another provider
To object
You can object to some uses, including direct marketing
About automated decisions
You can challenge some decisions made about you only by a computer
To complain
You can report a breach of your rights to the NDPC

You do not need a lawyer to use these rights. A clear, polite message that names the law, says exactly what you want, and gives the organisation a way to reply is usually enough to start. Organisations also have duties under the Act, such as keeping your data secure and collecting only what they need for a stated purpose.
How to use your rights
From problem to complaint
Write to the company
Keep copies and dates
Wait for a reply
Escalate to the regulator
Start with the organisation itself; a clear written record makes any later complaint much stronger.

Start with the organisation that holds your data or provides the service. Use its official email, app help section or customer care line, and put your request in writing so you have a record. Keep screenshots, dates and reference numbers. If it does not respond or does not fix the problem, take the complaint to the right regulator: the NDPC for misuse of personal data, the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC) for problems with your phone network, or the Central Bank of Nigeria's consumer protection channels for problems with banks, after you have complained to the bank first. Use only the contact details on the regulator's official website.
Worked example: stopping marketing calls from a company

For example, Ladi in Lafia once filled a form at a shop promotion. Months later, a company keeps calling and texting her with offers, and one message mentions her full name and home area. She wants to know what they hold and to stop the marketing.
She finds the company's official email in the privacy notice on its website.

She writes: "My name is Ladi (her surname), phone number (her number). Under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, please tell me what personal data you hold about me and where you got it, and stop using my data for direct marketing. Please confirm by email."
She saves the sent email and writes the date in her notebook.
The company replies, lists her name, number and area from the shop form, and confirms she has been removed from marketing.
If it had not replied, she was ready to send a complaint to the NDPC through its official website, attaching her email and screenshots of the calls.
In one short email Ladi used two rights, access and objection to direct marketing, and kept a record that would support a complaint if needed.
Your responsibilities
**Respect other people's privacy:** do not share their numbers, photos or private messages without consent.
**Respect other people's work:** do not post someone else's photos, designs or videos as your own; ask and give credit.
**Tell the truth:** check before you share, and correct mistakes.

**Be kind:** online insults, threats and harassment hurt real people. Nigeria's Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) Act 2015 makes serious online abuses, such as identity theft and cyberstalking, criminal offences.
**Protect the vulnerable:** help children, older relatives and new users set up safe phones and recognise scams.
Read before you tap Accept

When an app asks you to accept its terms or privacy policy, scroll to the parts about what data it collects and who it shares it with. Loan and betting apps in particular may ask for access to your contacts; think hard before allowing it.
Save a template
Keep a copy of a short data request message, like Ladi's, in your Notes app. When you need it, change the company name and send.

Step 2: write goals that can be checked

Keeping going when it gets hard

Most plans slip at some point: the phone gets lost, data runs out, a child falls ill. Plan for this. Keep your goals in a paper notebook as well as on the phone. If you miss a week, do not start again from zero; continue from where you stopped and move the deadline by one week. Your final project

Your course project brings three things together: a **digital safety checklist** you have completed on your own phone, **evidence of one digital task** you have done for real (for example a confirmed payment, a backed-up contact list, or a correction you posted to a group), and this **30-day digital goals plan**. Goal 3, growth: from day 15 to day 28, post 3 product photos with prices on Status each week: 3 posts a week times 2 weeks is 6 posts. Check: 6 posts and every sale recorded.

A small button phone makes calls and sends text messages. A smartphone does that too, but it is really a small computer. It goes on the internet, runs programs called apps, and takes good photos.

How to get online, and what the little icons at the top mean.

Before you buy
The four numbers that matter
Storage, for example 64 GB: room for photos
RAM, for example 4 GB: runs apps smoothly
Android version: newer stays safe longer
Storage is the space for apps, photos, videos and voice notes. Small storage fills up fast with WhatsApp photos.
RAM is the phone's working memory. Low RAM makes a phone slow.
The battery number, in mAh, tells you how much charge it holds. Bigger usually means longer use.
And the Android version. Newer versions get security updates for longer.
For example, Hauwa in Kano compares two phones at about the same price. Phone A has double the storage, double the RAM and 25% more battery, so she chooses it, and she asks for a written receipt.
Getting online
Mobile data or Wi-Fi?
Mobile data comes through your SIM card, and you pay for it with data bundles. Swipe down twice from the top and tap the Mobile data tile to switch it on.
Wi-Fi comes from a router, a MiFi, or another phone's hotspot. Long press the Wi-Fi tile, tap the network name, type the password exactly, and tap Connect.
On free Wi-Fi shared with strangers, do not open your bank app. Use your own data for anything with money.
Messages stuck?
Check the internet in this order
Signal first, then data switch, then balance.
Signal bars, and 4G or 3G, not E?
Mobile data on, with the right SIM?
Any data bundle left?
Still stuck? Restart the phone
For example, Grace in Port Harcourt sends three messages, but each shows a small clock instead of ticks. She reads the status bar, the thin strip at the top of the screen, before calling anyone.
First, is Airplane mode off?
Next, the signal. She has four bars and 4G, so the network is fine.
Then the data switch. There are no small arrows beside 4G. The Mobile data tile is grey, so she taps it on.
The messages are still stuck, so she checks her balance. Her bundle expired yesterday. She buys a new one, and the clocks turn to ticks.
If none of this works, switch Airplane mode on for ten seconds and off again, or restart the phone.
Safety first
Charging, battery and water
On a hard, open surface. Never under a pillow, on a bed or with wet hands. Use a good charger.
Back lifting or very hot? Stop using and charging it. Never press or pierce it. Take it for repair.
Switch it off. Do not charge it. Remove case and SIM tray. Air dry, no hairdryer or sun.

Most phone damage comes from heat, poor charging, drops and water. Charge on a table, never under a pillow or in a bag, and never with wet hands. When power returns after an outage, unplug the charger and wait for the power to settle.
If the back of your phone is lifting, or it gets very hot and smells strange, stop using and charging it at once. Never press or pierce a swollen battery. Take it to a qualified repairer.
If the phone gets wet, switch it off and do not charge it. Remove the case and SIM tray, and let it dry in open air for a long time. No hairdryer, oven or sun.
Once a week
Do these five checks once a week. Charger and cable undamaged. Screen protector not cracked. Charging port clean and dry, with no pin pushed in.
At least 15% of storage free, so the phone stays fast. And restart the phone once a week, which fixes many small problems.

A smartphone gives you more control over calls. You can put a call on speaker, mute yourself, or press 1 when a customer line asks.
SMS works on every phone with only airtime and signal.
WhatsApp lets you send voice notes, photos and calls over data.
And a backed-up contact list survives a lost phone. Let us see how, and how to stay safe.
Worked example
Saving a number in +234 format
0803 555 0142 has 11 digits
Remove the first 0
Put +234 in front
Save it and test the call
For example, Joy sells fabric in Aba. A customer writes her number on paper. Joy wants it to work for calls, SMS and WhatsApp, even when she travels. That needs the international format.
The number has 11 digits, starting with 0. This is a made-up example.
She removes the first 0.
She puts plus 234 in front. 234 is Nigeria's country code.
Now it has 13 digits after the plus sign.
She saves it under the customer's name and taps call to test it rings.
And remember, 112 is Nigeria's emergency number. You can dial it from the lock screen by tapping Emergency call.
Two kinds of message
SMS or WhatsApp?
Text only, 160 characters
WhatsApp
SMS needs no internet. One SMS holds 160 plain characters, but adding an emoji drops the limit to 70, so long messages and emoji can cost more.
A bank alert SMS is only a notice. Anyone can type a fake alert, so check your bank app before you release goods.
WhatsApp needs data or Wi-Fi, and both people need the app. It sends photos, voice notes and documents. Install it only from the Play Store.
WhatsApp ticks
How far has my message gone?
Clock: not sent yet, no internet
For example, Mama Nkechi in Owerri sends her son Emeka a message. First she sees a clock. That means it has not left her phone yet.
One grey tick means it is sent, but has not reached his phone.
Two grey ticks mean it arrived on his phone.
Two blue ticks mean he opened the chat. To send a voice note, she presses and holds the microphone, speaks, and lifts her finger.
Safety first
Codes that are for you alone
No bank, network or government office will call and ask for them. End the call.
Anyone who gets it can take your account. Never send it, even to a friend.
Got one you did not ask for? Do not share it. Change your password or call your bank.

No bank, network or government office will call and ask for your PIN, your password, or a code sent to your phone. If a caller asks, end the call, and call the organisation yourself on its official number.
Anyone who gets your WhatsApp verification code can take over your account. Never send it to anyone. Switch on two-step verification in WhatsApp settings too.
If a one-time code arrives that you did not ask for, someone may be trying to get into your account. Do not share it. And never dial a USSD code a stranger sends you to receive a payment.
Before you forward
Pause, check, then share or delete
If you cannot confirm it, do not forward it.
Pause: Forwarded many times?
Share the truth, or delete
For example, Patience in Benin City gets a message on Sunday night: all primary schools are closed tomorrow. It is marked Forwarded many times, with no date or office named.
She checks the state government's official page and the school's page. There is no announcement.
She calls the head teacher on the number from the school's letterhead. School is open as normal.
So instead of forwarding, she tells her parents' group of 60 members the truth. Sixty families were not misled by a rumour.

Save to your Google account
Add an emergency contact
Ask before sharing anyone's number

Install software updates
Run Google Play Protect

Know your rights online
A smartphone does not make money by itself. It helps you show what you sell, reach customers, take orders and receive payment.
It is also a classroom you can carry.
What you post builds trust, or costs you opportunities.
And you have rights online, just as you do offline. Let us see how to use all of this.
Worked example
Plantain chips sold on WhatsApp
For example, Adunni in Ibadan makes plantain chips and posts on WhatsApp Status every morning.
Price per pack
Cost per pack
Naira figures are approximate.
For example, Adunni in Ibadan makes plantain chips. She posts daylight photos with the price and how to order, and sells about 40 packs a week.
Each pack sells for about 1,000 naira.
Ingredients and packaging cost about 600 naira per pack.
So she makes 400 naira on each pack. That is 16,000 naira a week, and 64,000 naira over 4 weeks.
After about 5,000 naira for data, airtime and delivery, she earns about 59,000 naira a month. She records every sale, so she knows the real figure.
A screenshot, an SMS or a promise is not payment.
Show the product with a price
Take the order in writing
Customer pays by transfer or link
Confirm the money in your own app
Deliver, then record the sale
Show your product clearly, with the price.
Confirm every order in writing: item, quantity, total price and delivery day.
The customer pays by bank transfer, or to a licensed provider such as Opay, Moniepoint or PalmPay.
Now the most important step. Open your own bank or payment app, and see the money in your balance before you release goods.
Then deliver, and write the sale in your record: date, customer, item, amount, paid.
Easy money traps
Signs of a scheme, not a job
You must pay to join or buy a package
You earn by recruiting others who pay
Promises to double your money
Small pay first, then deposit to unlock
Pressure to act now, no real address
Genuine work pays you. Schemes take your money. Be suspicious if you must pay to join, if you earn by recruiting others, or if it promises to double your money.
Watch out when you are paid small amounts for easy tasks, then asked to deposit more to unlock earnings. If you are caught, stop paying, keep screenshots, and call your bank on its official number.

Download on Wi-Fi, watch later
Lower video quality to 360p or 480p
Use audio when you do not need the picture
Read text lessons
20 minutes a day, set as an alarm
Your phone is a classroom. To save data, download lessons on Wi-Fi and watch them offline.
Lower the video quality. For talking lessons, you lose little.
Listen to talks as audio while you cook or travel.
And read text lessons, which use far less data.
Make study a fixed appointment. For example, Rahila in Jos studies 20 minutes a day, five days a week. She counts reading and practice time, so she plans 6 weeks for her course.
